contributions.explanation: This theorem is the central result of the LATE framework. It shows that when treatment effects are heterogeneous and compliance is incomplete, the IV estimand—the ratio of the reduced-form effect to the first-stage effect—identifies the average causal effect for compliers, i.e., those who change treatment status in response to the instrument. The assumptions are: (1) the instrument is as good as randomly assigned, (2) the instrument has a nonzero effect on treatment (relevance), (3) the instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment (exclusion restriction), and (4) monotonicity, meaning no one is a defier (who would take treatment when assigned control but not when assigned treatment). This result clarifies what can be learned from IV designs and provides a transparent interpretation of the estimand.
limits: LATE is specific to compliers and may not generalize to other populations
Monotonicity may be violated in some settings
contributions.problem: With heterogeneous treatment effects and incomplete compliance, the IV estimand does not generally identify the average treatment effect for the whole population or the treated.

contributions.explanation: This representation is a key conceptual innovation. By framing IV in terms of potential outcomes, the source shows that the exogeneity assumption in linear regression actually combines two distinct assumptions: randomization (the instrument is independent of potential outcomes) and exclusion restriction (the instrument affects the outcome only through the treatment). This separation is important because violations of these assumptions have different sources and consequences. For example, in the schooling example, birth date is plausibly random, but it may affect earnings through school starting age, violating exclusion. This framework allows researchers to assess the plausibility of each assumption separately and to conduct sensitivity analyses.
